title: Octopus, Octopi, Octopod, Octopuses
summary: Josh and Chuck discuss octopuses: the Paul the octopus World Cup prediction story, plural forms (octopi, octopuses, octopods), cephalopod classification, the mantle and funnel/siphon, blue hemocyanin blood and three hearts, chromatophore color change and camouflage, ink defense, eyes and the camera lens spinoff, jet propulsion, solitary den life, sucker sensitivity and arm nervous systems, beak, radula and salivary papilla for drilling shells, reproduction (male pillow octopus hectocotylus, female brooding and death), intelligence, personality studies by Roland Anderson and Jennifer Mather, and problem solving. Ends with listener mail about customs and cigars and tour announcements for an Atlanta trivia event.

segments.title: Opening banter and Paul the World Cup octopus
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with small talk, then Josh introduces Paul the octopus from a German sea life center, who picked the winners of World Cup matches by eating mussels from one of two boxes.

segments.title: Plural forms and classification
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether to say octopi, octopuses, or octopods, then classify octopuses as mollusks in class Cephalopoda, with squid and nautilus, noting they lack an outer shell and the name means head-foot.

segments.title: Anatomy: mantle, eyes, and funnel
segments.summary: The mantle, the bulbous sack behind the eyes, holds the internal organs and is a strong muscle that aids respiration. The funnel, also called a siphon, is introduced.

segments.title: Blue blood and three hearts
segments.summary: Octopus blood is blue because it uses hemocyanin, a copper-based protein, instead of iron-based hemoglobin. Octopuses have three hearts, two pumping blood to the gills and one for the body.

segments.title: Color change and chromatophores
segments.summary: Octopuses change color using chromatophores, small pigment sacs controlled individually by nerves, along with reflective iridophores and papillae that alter texture. The hosts describe videos of the camouflage and compare it to chameleons.

segments.title: Ink, evasion, and mimicry
segments.summary: Octopuses release ink and jet water from the funnel to evade predators, and the ink contains a substance that impairs a predator's taste and smell. They can also change their shape to mimic other animals, such as a sea snake in front of a damselfish.

segments.title: Brain, nervous system, and arm independence
segments.summary: The octopus brain is large relative to body size and its arms hold most of its nerves. Researchers severed arm nerves and tickled the arms to show each arm can act with its own nervous system.

segments.title: Eyes, camera lens research, and jet propulsion
segments.summary: Octopus eyes have layered corneas that inspired camera lens designs, reducing camera costs. Octopuses can jet through water using the siphon, reaching about 20 mph, though not out of water.

segments.title: Solitary life, dens, and walking with suckers
segments.summary: Octopuses live alone in dens and move to a new den every couple of weeks for unknown reasons. They walk using their suckers, which are very sensitive with about ten thousand neurons each.

segments.title: Beak, radula, and salivary papilla
segments.summary: Octopuses have a parrot-like beak and a barbed tongue called a radula used to scrape meat from shells. They also have a salivary papilla that can be shot out to drill shells, and secretions that erode the shell to make drilling easier.

segments.title: Octopus reproduction and the male pillow octopus
segments.summary: Male pillow octopuses are tiny compared to females, and the male uses a hectocotylus arm to transfer sperm, often breaking it off and dying within months. The female broods eggs for months without eating and dies after they hatch. Hatchling survival is very low.

segments.title: Personality, problem solving, and tool use
segments.summary: Researchers Roland Anderson and Jennifer Mather found octopuses show distinct personalities, citing aquarium octopuses named Leisure Suit Larry, Emily Dickinson, and Lucretia. Octopuses also solved a wired-shut clam problem and some use tools.
